result:
## REJECT for recording.

Four blocking defects. Three are fixable in a single revision pass; none require new research or new results.

---

### Blocking

**1. The project name and the company name are homophones aloud.**

> "At bet three sixty five, we have started building on one of them, in a project we call bet three sixty fly."

Spoken, "bet three sixty five" and "bet three sixty fly" are near-identical. As a first-time listener I heard the company name said twice and did not register a pun — which left the project with no audible name for the remaining ten minutes. Every later reference ("the first engineering problem in bet three sixty fly") then floats free. This is the one defect that exists *only* in the audio medium, and it's structural: either the name gets an explicit beat ("...a project we call bet three sixty *fly* — with a fly, as in fruit fly"), or the narration needs a short handle it can use throughout. Related smaller wrinkle: the pun arrives one paragraph before the listener is told the animal is a fruit fly.

**2. The piece never states what it is for, so the headline result lands as failure.**

The stated outcome is:

> "the frozen pipeline called about fifty-six percent of them correctly, level with a conventional model given the same pregame information"

A listener who has been led here by "What could you build...?" hears: *you built a fly brain to predict baseball and it did no better than the normal thing.* The script's actual thesis — that this is an interpretability testbed, and parity is the point because it buys you a season of inspectable responses — doesn't appear until the sentences *after* the number. One sentence planted back at the bet365 mention ("we were not trying to beat a baseball model; we were trying to get one we could take apart") converts that paragraph from a letdown into the payoff, and it retroactively justifies the entire back half.

Compounding it: **fifty-six percent has no scale attached.** The listener has no idea whether that is impressive, ordinary, or barely above guessing. One clause of anchoring is required — you have the number, I'm not asking you to invent one.

**3. The script raises its best question and drops it.**

> "If you work with embeddings, the shape will be familiar: something goes in, a representation comes out of the middle, a head reads the representation."

This is the strongest explanatory sentence in the piece — **do not cut it.** But it hands an attentive listener the obvious objection and then walks away: if a small external model fit on past seasons does the predicting, is the connectome contributing anything, or would any fixed scramble of wiring in the middle score the same? The narration has already told me the middle is "a circuit with an anatomy," which is exactly the claim in question. It needs one sentence closing the loop — whatever the honest answer is, including "we haven't run that control yet." Leaving it open is the difference between a listener who is persuaded and one who spends the next three paragraphs arguing with you.

**4. The DOOMFLY digression is defensive and breaks the spine of the piece.**

> "That code path is also how you tell a project like DOOMFLY apart from the flies crawling around people's feeds, because some of those are animations — a fly wanders a browser window with a dopamine meter ticking beside it, the behavior written in JavaScript, no neural model making any of the decisions."

This is a long, syntactically tangled sentence that asks the listener to hold "code path" as an abstract referent, and its content is a swipe at unnamed other people. It reads as anxiety about being mistaken for them. Aloud it stalls the momentum right where the Doom section should be accelerating. Cut it, or reduce it to the one clean idea it contains: *the question is what controls the next movement.*

---

### Required but not blocking

**The final line is broken.**

> "As the maps grow... we will have much more of that animal's solution available to work with. The fly is where we can start building that experience today."

"That experience" has no antecedent — the preceding noun is "solution." The closing sentence of a narration cannot have a dangling referent; it's the line people carry out. The callback structure before it ("We started with the question...") is good and should stay.

**The back third sags.** The piece runs roughly eleven to twelve minutes read aloud. FlyVis, FlyBody, Fish2, ZAPBench, and MICrONS arrive as five proper nouns across three paragraphs, none of them the speaker's own work, and none of them teaching the listener a new idea. This is where attention goes. The mammalian paragraph also ends on its own thesis ("what carries across is the practice") immediately before the real conclusion restates it — a double ending. Compressing this material into a single forward-looking paragraph would cost nothing and buy back two minutes.

**Two weak seams.** The results paragraph begins cold on "Across the two thousand four hundred and twenty-three games..." with no signal that we've moved from method to outcome. And the learning section hangs off a single word:

> "A living fly **also** carries the previous encounter into the next one."

That "also" is the only thing connecting it to what came before, and the paragraph ends on a hedge — "Those learned connections give us another part of the model to investigate in the sports experiments" — which tells me it isn't actually used yet. Either tighten the link or move the section.

**Opaque phrasings, spoken.** "In a separate development model we built that in" is unparseable on first hearing. "Frozen pipeline" is unglossed ML jargon in a script that carefully defines *synapse* and *ventral nerve cord*. "A small external model fit on past seasons" — "fit" as a verb will be heard as the adjective.

**Production note.** The script consistently spells numbers for the reader ("two thousand four hundred and twenty-three," "fifty-six percent"), then breaks convention with "the 2023 Major League Baseball season."

**One gap the listener will notice.** A betting company describes building a baseball prediction system and never says whether it touches real odds. The script doesn't have to answer that, but the silence is audible.

---

### What's working — keep it

The transition craft is genuinely good. "What an engineer downloads at the end of all that is a graph," "Which brings us to the awkward part," and "Once you have an adapter into the circuit, you can give it a different environment" all do real work with no filler. The rhetorical flourish earns its place:

> "Nobody drew that layout on a whiteboard. It is there because it kept flies alive."

Prerequisite ordering in the first half is close to ideal — neuron, synapse, connectome, scale, acquisition, graph, dynamics, adapter — each term is available before it's needed.

**Audience consistency is a deliberate strength, not an accident.** The script explains all biology from zero and assumes fluency in ML ("embeddings," "a head reads the representation"). That is a coherent target — an engineering audience reading into neuroscience — and it holds from the first paragraph to the last. "Frozen pipeline" is the only term that sits outside it in either direction.

The honesty about parity is also right, and I'd keep it verbatim. The problem is placement, not candor.
